title: Carbohydrates in Nutrition

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of carbohydrates like LEGO structures. A monosaccharide is a single LEGO brick, the smallest piece you can have. When you snap two bricks together you get a disaccharide, and when you connect a whole bunch you get a polysaccharide. Everything sugary is built from those single bricks, called monosaccharides.

### Question 2

Your body is like a car, and carbohydrates are the fuel it likes best because it burns clean and fast. Your brain especially runs almost entirely on this fuel (glucose). Protein is more like the metal that builds the car body, but carbs are what keep it running.

### Question 3

Every gram of carbohydrate hands your body about 4 little energy coins (kilocalories). Protein also gives 4, but fat is the big spender at 9. So if you want to remember: carbs and protein are the 4-coin foods, and fat is the 9-coin food.

### Question 4

Fiber is a carbohydrate, but it is locked with a special kind of clasp that human stomachs do not have the right key (enzyme) to open. So instead of being unlocked and used for energy, it travels through and helps sweep your digestive system clean. It is a carb your body cannot cash in.

### Question 5

Simple carbs are like a single bead or a pair of beads, quick and small. Complex carbs are a long necklace of many beads strung together, like starch in bread and potatoes. The word complex is your clue: it just means a longer, more built-up chain of sugar beads.

### Question 6

When you have more sugar (glucose) than you need right now, your body packs it into a storage bundle called glycogen, like putting extra snacks in a backpack. Later, when you run low on energy, you unzip the backpack and grab the sugar back out fast. It is your quick-access energy stash.

### Question 7

Fiber acts like a speed bump for sugar entering your blood. Whole grains still have their fiber speed bumps, so the sugar trickles in slowly. Refined grains and sweet drinks have the speed bumps removed, so the sugar rushes in all at once. Slow and steady is what fiber gives you.

### Question 8

Complex carbs are the long-chain sugar foods, like the starch in brown rice. Honey, table sugar, and candy are all short, quick sugars, the beads that come alone or in pairs. So when you want a complex carb, reach for grains and starchy foods, not the sweet stuff.

### Question 9

The Total Carbohydrate line on a label is like a basket holding three things: starch, sugars, and fiber. Fiber sits in the carb basket even though it is not sweet. Fat and protein have their own separate baskets on the label, so they do not belong here.

### Question 10

If the sugar (glucose) runs low, your body does not just give up, it improvises. It tears down some protein to build new glucose, and it starts burning fat in a special way that makes backup fuel called ketones. Eating enough carbs means your body does not have to raid its protein to keep going, which is called protein sparing.

### Question 11

Two foods can both give you energy, but one comes with a bonus and one comes empty-handed. Fruit and whole grains bring their carbs plus fiber and vitamins, like a gift that has extra presents packed inside. Added sugars bring pretty much just the energy and no bonus, which is why they are called empty calories and why the nutrition guidelines say to keep them to a minimum instead of making them part of your regular meals.

### Question 12

Starch and glycogen are basically the same idea, a big bundle of glucose beads saved for later, but they live in different places. Plants stash their glucose as starch, and animals (including you) stash it as glycogen. Same job, different address.
